previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with recurrent substernal chest pain radiating to the left shoulder, concerning for unstable angina given her history of multiple NSTEMIs. Initial evaluation showed no troponin elevation or EKG changes, but due to persistent symptoms, she underwent cardiac catheterization which revealed chronic total occlusion of the OM1 and OM2 arteries without intervention possible. She was managed medically with continuation of dual antiplatelet therapy, beta-blockade, and initiation of isosorbide mononitrate for anginal prophylaxis. Her kidney function remained stable with a mild, expected rise in creatinine post-catheterization; nephrology was involved to ensure safe contrast use and medication management. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans for outpatient follow-up in cardiology and nephrology, including repeat renal labs.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ y/o female with a history of FSGN s/p renal 
transplant in ___, DVT/PE previously on coumadin but stopped

# Chest pain: Patient has known history of coronary artery 
disease and medically managed NSTEMIs with recent cath in ___ 
with no intervenable lesions but presents with non-exertional 
chest pain not responsive to SL Nitroglycerin. EKG without 
changes, first troponin negative. Patient with known CAD without 
interventions. Ranolazine was started this admission to maximize 
anti-anginal regimen. However, unclear that chest pain was 
changed with this medication, would recommend re-assesing 
utility as outpatient with cardiologist. Other concerns were 
recurrent PE, gastritis or musculoskeletal origin. PE was ruled 
out with VQ scan (obtained to prevent renal injury), gastritis 
was unlikely as no improvement noted with GI cocktail 
(Maalox/diphenhydramine/lidocaine).  Given lack of response to 
nitroglycerin and improvement with anti-inflammatories and 
narcotics, concern was increased for musculoskeletal origin of 
chest pain.

# CKD s/p renal transplant: Cr 2.5, baseline 1.6-1.9 though 
recently in the 2.3-2.5 range. Transplant nephrology followed 
during hospitalization. Was continued on home tacrolimus and 
sirolimus though levels slightly sub therapeutic during 
admission (though this was attributed to not taking medications 
while in the emergency department).

# Anemia: likely somewhat related to chronic renal disease, at 
baseline. Iron studies on last admission showed iron of 35 and 
ferritin of 31. Given low MCV and iron/ferritin on lower side 
would likely benefit from iron repletion. Continued home folic 
acid. Would consider iron repletion as an outpatient
# Gout: continued home febuxostat  
# Depression: continued home citalopram

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms ___, 

It was a pleasure taking care of you at ___. 
You presented with chest pain. Given your history of pulmonary 
embolism, we obtained a scan that showed that this was very 
unlikely to be the cause of chest pain. Given your history of 
coronary artery disease, we checked labs which showed you were 
not having a heart attack. We added a new cardiac medication, 
Ranexa, to address possible anginal pain, but it actually seems 
like your pain responded best to pain medications, so we think 
it may actually be musculoskeletal. We recommend close follow up 
with your cardiologist for a possible repeat stress test as an 
outpatient. 

We held your home lasix in setting of kidney injury, with 
improvement. We will have you have repeat labs within a week of 
discharge to re-evaluate kidney function, and check weight 
daily; if weight increases >3lbs, please call physician.
